claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys can retain attractive mechanical properties at temperatures from about 800°C to 1500°C.
High configurational entropy favors formation of a solid-solution phase in high-entropy alloys.
NbTaHfTiZr or NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 can serve as a disordered, single-phase BCC refractory solid solution.
Multiple principal elements inherently produce lattice distortions in the proposed alloys.
A high density of edge dislocations predominantly governs elevated-temperature strength retention in refractory BCC HEAs.
A high density of edge dislocations predominantly governs elevated-temperature thermoelastic behavior in refractory BCC HEAs.
High configurational entropy gives rise to elastic anisotropy that modulates edge-dislocation mobility.
Systematic composition changes can tune elastic anisotropy and the dislocation contrast factor.
Neutron-diffraction peak broadening can reveal deformation-generated substructures that include dislocations.
Line broadening and contrast-factor measurements can specifically quantify the density and behavior of edge dislocations.
Increasing elastic anisotropy through alloying raises the energy barrier for edge-dislocation glide.
Reduced edge-dislocation mobility can provide high-temperature strength retention in BCC HEAs.
Reduced dislocation mobility limits plastic accommodation and thereby modifies thermal expansion behavior.
Alloy variants with greater elastic anisotropy will have a higher effective density of pinned edge dislocations.
Alloy variants with greater elastic anisotropy will retain more high-temperature yield strength than baseline variants.
Alloy variants with greater elastic anisotropy will exhibit reduced thermal-expansion anomalies relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies only to disordered BCC refractory HEAs and not to non-BCC or multiphase alloys.
Edge-dislocation strengthening is more capable of providing high-temperature strength retention than screw-dislocation strengthening.
Grain size, deformation substructures, or minor secondary phases may affect whether edge dislocations dominate the mechanical and thermoelastic response.
